metadata.title: Research engagement in the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study: A systematic review

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a systematic review of PIRLS-related research articles rather than an analysis of PIRLS microdata. As such, it does not construct an analytic student sample from PIRLS, does not apply IEA/OECD complex survey weights, and does not use plausible values for achievement outcomes. The review’s “sampling” refers to the article-identification and screening process (database searches, deduplication, inclusion/exclusion criteria), not to a survey design with student-level weights. Therefore, no PIRLS weight variables (e.g., student design weights or replicate weights) are applicable to the reported results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this study does not estimate cognitive achievement scores from PIRLS microdata; it synthesizes and categorizes findings from previously published PIRLS-related articles. The review does not perform an imputation or deletion procedure for missing item responses or questionnaire variables because it does not analyze individual-level PIRLS responses. Instead, it uses bibliographic search and coding procedures to describe trends in the literature.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The unit of analysis is PIRLS-related peer-reviewed articles, not students. The authors built a database starting from Lenkeit et al. (2004–2015; 113 articles) and added new articles via searches in ERIC, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, and Zetoc using PIRLS/Progress in International Reading Literacy Study terms, restricted to January 2015–May 2022. They excluded non-peer-reviewed items, non-English versions when an English peer-reviewed copy could not be located, conference proceedings, articles where PIRLS was not the main focus (screened via abstract and then full text keyword checks), and studies using PIRLS materials on smaller independent samples or commentaries on other PIRLS-related research. Reliability checks were conducted on randomly selected subsets of newly located articles (25 for 2015–2018; 25 for 2019–2022), followed by plausibility/completeness checks across all 221 articles in the final database.

The review reports descriptive patterns in the literature rather than predictive modeling results: it quantifies how research engagement has changed over time, which PIRLS cycles are most used (notably 2011 and 2016), and how article “nature” (secondary analysis, critiques, impact/policy) and thematic foci vary. It also summarizes qualitative themes in three areas: teacher characteristics/instruction practices, socioeconomic predictors of reading outcomes, and critiques of PIRLS scaling/IRT practices. Because the study does not train or evaluate ML models on PIRLS microdata, there are no model performance metrics, no survey-weighted estimation, and no plausible-value handling for achievement outcomes. data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a systematic review rather than an empirical ML paper. Consequently, there is no student-level dataset, no analytic sample size, no country-level sample counts, no plausible-value generation/combining, and no missing-data handling for PIRLS responses. The absence of main findings rows and ML techniques is expected because the study’s results are bibliographic/descriptive (coding and synthesis of prior research) rather than model-based prediction or causal estimation.
